UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                     BEFORE THE
                       FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

                                                       )    Docket Nos.
    El Paso Natural Gas Company, LLC                   )    CP26-558-000
                                                       )    CP82-435-000

                               Answer to Motion to Dismiss Protest

          On July 30, 2026, El Paso Natural Gas Company, LLC (“EPNG”) submitted a Request

for Prior Notice Authorization seeking authorization to construct the McCloud Lateral Project

pursuant to a blanket certificate. The McCloud Lateral Project (“Project”) would consist of a new

5.8 mile, 16-inch gas pipeline in El Paso County, Texas that would deliver 167,000 Dekatherms

per day of gas to a new power generation facility that would power the proposed Meta El Paso

data center. On October 5, 2026, Sierra Club and Food & Water Watch (collectively, “Movants”)

filed a protest and motion to intervene pursuant to 18 C.F.R. § 157.205(e).1 EPNG filed an

answer to the protest on October 9, 2026, and moved to dismiss Movant’s protest.2

          Given the Commission’s prohibition against answers to protests under 18 C.F.R. §

385.213(a)(2), Movants respectfully request that the Director of the Office of Energy Projects

reject EPNG’s answer and reject the filing in its entirety. However, if the Director accepts the

filing, Movants respectfully file this answer to the motion to dismiss.3



1
  Sierra Club and Food & Water Watch, Joint Protest and Motion to Intervene, Docket No. CP26-
558-000 (filed Oct. 5, 2026) (“Joint Protest”).
2
  El Paso Natural Gas Company, Motion for Leave to Answer, Answer and Motion to Dismiss
Protest, Docket No. CP 26-558-000 (filed Oct. 9, 2026) (“Motion to Dismiss”).
3
  If necessary, Movants ask for leave to file an answer pursuant to FERC Rules of Practice and
Procedure 212 and 213 (18 C.F.R. §§ 385.212, 385.213).




                                                 1
          As set forth below, Movants’ protest meets the requirements of 18 C.F.R. § 157.205(e),

and EPNG fails to provide any compelling reason to dismiss the protest or waive the 30-day

reconciliation period. As such, EPNG’s motion should be denied.

         I.     Movants condemn individual commenters’ violent language
         On October 5, 2026, Sierra Club submitted a batch of 350 digital comments of members

and supporters concerned about the McCloud Lateral project.4 As EPNG’s motion points out,

two of those contained inappropriate and violent language. Movants emphatically condemn any

calls for violence, and agree that such language has no place in Commission proceedings. Sierra

Club routinely screens all public comments for any such objectionable language, and did so in

this instance, but failed to catch these two comments. Upon learning of the two comments, Sierra

Club removed them from the FERC docket, and has since taken steps to improve their screening

practices to ensure that no violent or offensive language is included in any future submissions to

Commission dockets.

         II.    Movants’ protest meets the Commission’s requirements for blanket
                certificate proceedings
         Under 18 C.F.R. § 157.205(e), any person may file a protest involving a “detailed

statement of Protestor's interest in the activity and the specific reasons and rationale for the

objection and whether the protestor seeks to be an intervener.” Further, a protest may only be

dismissed “if it does not raise a substantive issue and fails to provide any specific detailed reason

or rationale for the objection.” 18 C.F.R. § 157.205(g). Applying this standard, Movants’ protest

should be accepted.

         In their protest, Movants have thoroughly detailed the interests that Sierra Club and Food

& Water Watch hold in the Project, how each organization, as well as each organizations’


4
    Sierra Club, Comments, Docket No. CP26-558-000 (filed Oct. 5, 2026).
                                                  2
 members, stand to be harmed by the construction and operation of the Project. See, e.g., Joint

Protest, 3-11, 16-20. Movants have also set forth specific, substantive concerns about the projects

and the rationale for their objections. Id. For example, Movants explain that the Project would

have adverse impacts to the air quality and water supplies of nearby communities; that the

cumulative impacts of this project combined with other past, present and reasonably-foreseeable

projects would be significant; and that these impacts would disproportionately impact Chaparral,

a predominately Hispanic and low-income community that continues to be burdened with

pollution from industrial projects on all sides. Id at 3-11.

       Because Movants provided a statement of their interest in the project and specific reasons

and rationale for the objection, they have met the protest requirements of § 157.205(e). Pursuant

to §157.205(f), EPNG’s request for blanket certificate authorization should therefore be treated

as an application authorization under section 7 of the Natural Gas Act (“NGA”).

       EPNG advances several arguments for dismissal that are without merit. First, it

mischaracterizes Movant’s concerns as “generalized objections to the development of natural gas

and data center infrastructure.” Motion to Dismiss, at 1. This is inaccurate. As set above,

Movants have raised concerns about the potential adverse impacts to air quality, noise, water, and

socioeconomics from the construction and operation of the Project itself; all of which would be

exacerbated by the cumulative effects of the Project combined with other past, present, and

future industrial projects in the immediate vicinity of the Project. See, e.g., Joint Protest, 3-5.

        These specific concerns about the Project meet the requirements of § 157.205(e), and

EPNG fails to provide any authority in support of their argument that the protest should be

dismissed over what they call generalized concerns. Moreover, the primary Commission decision

on which EPNG relies is readily distinguishable. In Kinder Morgan Interstate Gas Transmission



                                                   3
 LLC, 133 FERC ¶ 61,044, at 61,196, a pipeline company called Seminole protested Kinder

Morgan’s use of a blanket certificate for a small pipeline Kinder Morgan had purchased.

Seminole wanted Kinder Morgan to purchase its pipeline, instead, and sought a FERC hearing to

determine which pipeline purchase was the lowest-cost option. The Commission dismissed

Seminole’s protest because it could not grant the relief sought—it had no authority to order

Kinder Morgan to purchase Seminole’s pipeline, and therefore would not hold a hearing on the

matter. By contrast here, Movants have raised legitimate environmental concerns over the

Project and the impacts it would have on surrounding local communities, and the Commission

can and should review the pipeline under the NGA section 7 review process.

       EPNG’s motion also goes to great lengths arguing that Movants’ concerns fall outside the

scope of the Commission’s NEPA obligations, and therefore their protest should be dismissed.

Motion to Dismiss, at 6-13. That is a red herring, and an attempt to raise the bar for protests

beyond what is required by § 157.205(e). That regulation implementing the NGA blanket

certificate program set a relatively low threshold for protests: it requires only that protesters raise

specific and substantive concerns with the project, which Movants have done here. It does not

require that those issues be limited to NEPA deficiencies; nor does § 157.205(g) state that the

Commission should dismiss a protest if the issues raised are outside the scope of the agency’s

NEPA obligations.

       Indeed, filing a protest that raises objections to a project triggers the NGA section 7

process, where FERC must consider whether the project “is or will be required by the present or

future public convenience and necessity…” 15 U.S.C. § 717f(e). While the Commission’s NEPA

analysis is a part of that determination, the Commission’s section 7 inquiry is broader. The

Commission’s regulations governing protests of blanket certificate authorizations do not provide



                                                   4
 for the litigation of factual or NEPA disputes. See 18 C.F.R. § 157.205(f)-(g). Such questions are

reserved for the Commission’s section 7 review process.

        Finally, EPNG incorrectly suggest that Movants’ protest constitutes an “attempted abuse

of the Commission’s blanket certificate program” which is intended to fast-track “non-

controversial construction projects.” Motion to Dismiss, at 2-3. But notwithstanding EPNG’s

self-serving characterization of its own project, Commission regulations set forth the test for

whether a project is “non-controversial” such that it can proceed under a blanket certificate:

whether any party files a protest. If that low threshold is met, the project is per se controversial

enough to require a NGA section 7 review. Here, as set forth above, Movants have filed a valid

protest that explains their interests in the project and objections to blanket certification. In

addition, Sierra Club and Friends of the Earth each filed group comments of several hundreds of

citizens in NM and TX that are opposed to the project. This demonstrates that there are

legitimate public concerns with the Project, including but not limited to its contribution to

cumulative effects from numerous projects in the area surrounding Chaparral, NM.

        As such, Movants protested blanket certificate authorization, which dictates a full section

7 review process under the Commission’s regulations. There is nothing improper about following

Commission protest procedures, and absolutely no merit to the suggestion that it constitutes an

abuse of the process.

        III.    EPNG’s request to waive the 30-day reconciliation period should be denied.
        EPNG further requests that the Commission waive the 30-day reconciliation period set

forth in § 157.205(f). However, the Commission regulations do not contain any provisions for

waiver of that procedural step to expedite a project, and EPNG has failed to articulate a reason

for the Commission to expedite the matter here.

        Commission Rule 205(g) states:

                                                   5
        Within 10 days of the filing of a protest, the Director of the Office of Energy Projects will
       dismiss that protest if it does not raise a substantive issue and fails to provide any specific
       detailed reason or rationale for the objection.
18 C.F.R. § 157.205(g). Further, Rule 205(f) states:

       If a protest is filed in accordance with paragraph (e) of this section, then the certificate
       holder, the person who filed the protest, any intervenors, and staff shall have 30 days
       from the deadline determined in accordance with paragraph (d) of this section, to resolve
       the protest, and to file a withdrawal of the protest pursuant to paragraph (g) of this
       section. Informal settlement conferences may be convened by the Director of the Office
       of Energy Projects or his designee. If a protest is not withdrawn or dismissed pursuant to
       paragraph (g) of this section, the activity shall not be deemed authorized by the blanket
       certificate. Instead, the request filed by the certificate holder shall be treated as an
       application for section 7 authorization for the particular activity.
18 C.F.R. § 157.205(f).

       Thus, the Commission regulations set out a clear procedure regarding protests to blanket

certificate authorizations: if the Commission seeks to dismiss a protest, it must do so within 10

days of the protest being filed. If the Commission does not dismiss the protest within 10 days,

the 30-day reconciliation period shall proceed. And, if Movants do not withdraw their protest

within the 30-day period, the request by the certificate holder shall then be treated as an

application for section 7 authorization.

       Movants filed their protest in the instant docket on October 5, 2026, and the Commission

did not dismiss Movants’ protest within the 10-day dismissal window set forth in Rule 205(g).

Even if Commission rules allowed EPNG to seek waiver of the reconciliation period, which they

do not, EPNG has failed to set forth any compelling reason to do so here. For example, they fail

to explain the permitting status and/or construction timeline of the proposed power generation

facility that the McCloud Lateral would serve, or the expected completion date of the Meta El

Paso data center. In fact, EPNG states no reason at all for its urgency.




                                                  6
        To the extent EPNG has planned for or relied on an expedited blanket certificate

authorization to meet a certain in-service date, they have assumed the risk that individuals and/or

groups would file protests and a full section 7 review would be required.

Conclusion

       For the reasons stated above, EPNG’s Motion to Dismiss and Request for Waiver of the

30-day Reconciliation Period should be denied.

Submitted: October 26, 2026
